title: The Undisturbed One-pointed Mind in Practice and the Undisturbed One-pointed Mind in Principle
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: What is one-pointed mind in practice and one-pointed mind in principle?

inline.s: Question: What is one-pointed mind in practice and one-pointed mind in principle?

Answer: One-pointed mind in practice and one-pointed mind in principle are also called “undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice” and “undisturbed one-pointed mind in principle.” Reciting the name of the Buddha has both a holding in practice and a holding in principle. Holding in practice is reciting Amitabha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; holding in principle is reciting the Buddha of one's own nature (the Amitabha of one's own nature). Holding in practice is aimed directly at rebirth; holding in principle is aimed at seeing one's nature. In the “Inscription on the Stupa of Master Lianchi Hong of Yunqi,” composed by Master Hanshan Deqing, it is recorded: “
Question: Can one gain awakening by reciting the Buddha's name
(seeing one's nature)
? The Master
(Master Lianchi)
replied: ‘Turn back the hearing to hear your own nature, and your nature becomes the unsurpassed Way. What doubt, then, that turning back the recitation recites your own nature?’
” Master Yinguang said: “
Turn back the recitation to recite your own nature, and your nature becomes the unsurpassed Way.
” (Master Yinguang's Collected Letters, vol. 4, “Second Letter in Reply to Layman Qi Zhizhou.”)

Holding in principle must be carried out on the foundation of a holding in practice that has already achieved undisturbed one-pointed mind; only thus can one avoid the calamity of falling into emptiness. Master Yinguang said: “

Because of the Amitabha of one's own nature, one must recite the Amitabha of the West so as to seek rebirth, and by gradual progress one can personally realize the Amitabha of one's own nature. If one clings solely to the Amitabha of one's own nature and does not recite the Amitabha of the West, then even if one truly awakens
(illumines the mind and sees one's nature)
, one is still not yet able to end birth and death at once
(if the delusions of views and thoughts are not cut off, one cannot end birth and death)
” (Master Yinguang's Collected Letters, “Answers to Twenty-seven Questions from Layman Qu Tianxiang.”)

[The delusions of views and thoughts] The delusions of views and the delusions of thoughts. The delusions of views are the errors of understanding held by ordinary beings, such as the five wrong views: the view of a self, the extreme view, the deviant view, the view of clinging to views, and the view of clinging to precepts and prohibitions. The delusions of thoughts are the errors of thinking held by ordinary beings, namely the afflictions of greed, hatred, ignorance, arrogance, and doubt. These two kinds of delusion are the root by which sentient beings drift through the three realms and suffer birth and death in vain; cutting them off, one can end birth and death and leave the three realms.
Holding in principle is reciting the Buddha of one's own nature (the Amitabha of one's own nature) so as to see through to one's original face. Master Lianchi said: “
You should know that the Pure Land is mind only; there is no realm outside it.
Speaking from principle, one's own nature returning to its original substance is the meaning of vowing to be born in that land.

Reciting the Buddha is reciting the mind; being born there is not apart from being born here. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are one substance; one does not dwell in the middle current or on either shore. Hence it is said: the Amitabha of one's own nature, the Pure Land that is mind only.
” (Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra.)

[Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are one substance] Buddha and sentient beings are two states of the mind: when the mind awakens, it is Buddha; when the mind is deluded, it is a sentient being. [One does not dwell in the middle current or on either shore] Master Lianchi explains in his Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra: “

By ‘the middle current and the two shores,’ Sahā is a metaphor for this shore and Ultimate Bliss for the other. At first one detests suffering and delights in bliss; then both suffering and bliss vanish; and in the end one does not dwell even in that which is neither suffering nor bliss. This is what is meant by not attaching to either extreme and not resting in the middle way.
” [Not resting in the middle way] Not dwelling in that which is neither suffering nor bliss.
Concerning holding in practice and holding in principle, Master Lianchi taught: “

To recall and recollect without interruption is called holding in practice; to investigate and examine without interruption is called holding in principle. These shall be discussed in detail below and taken as the cause. The one-pointed mind that comes later
(the undisturbed one-pointed mind spoken of later)

also has its practice aspect and its principle aspect. Those who do not understand this think that reciting the Buddha's name is only for those of dull faculties and that only investigating Chan can bring awakening. Beginners who hear this cannot decide for themselves. They do not know that investigating while reciting the Buddha's name is extremely close in meaning to the way the worthy elders of former generations taught people to raise a huatou and cultivate the sensation of doubt. Hence it is said that in investigating Chan one need not raise a separate huatou; it is enough to apply oneself to the single phrase “Amitabha Buddha.” How wonderful are these words!
” (Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra.)

[The one-pointed mind that comes later also has a practice aspect and a principle aspect.] The undisturbed one-pointed mind spoken of later also includes the undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice and the undisturbed one-pointed mind in principle. Master Ouyi said: “

The one-pointed mind in practice is when each recitation is distinctly clear, without dullness or scattering. The one-pointed mind in principle is silently according with the unborn and penetratingly understanding one's own nature.
” (The Lingfeng Collection,
“Occasional Talks in the Brahma Room.”) [Thinking recitation is only for those of dull faculties] To think that reciting the Buddha's name is suited only to people of dull faculties.
Concerning the undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice and the undisturbed one-pointed mind in principle, Master Lianchi continued:
“(Reciting the name of the Buddha)

is divided into practice and principle: to recall and recollect without interruption is called holding in practice; to investigate and examine without interruption is called holding in principle. ‘To recall and recollect’ means that on hearing the Buddha's name one constantly recalls and constantly recites it, tracing it with the mind, each syllable distinct, the former phrase and the latter phrase continuing without break. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is only this one thought and no second thought, unmixed by thoughts of greed, hatred, and affliction. This is what the Sūtra of the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance means when it says: ‘In solitude and stillness, one's mind is single; amid the throng of afflictions, one's mind is single; even in places of praise or blame, gain or loss, good or evil, one's mind is single.’ When one has attained it in practice but has not yet penetrated it in principle, gaining only the power of faith and not yet having seen the Way, this is called the one-pointed mind in practice.

‘To investigate and examine’ means that on hearing the Buddha's name, one not only recalls and recollects it, but turns the recitation back to contemplate, observing, examining, and investigating to trace it to its root. When this investigation reaches its limit, it suddenly accords with one's own original mind. Within this there are again two aspects. First, suchness and wisdom are non-dual: apart from the mind that can recite, there is no Buddha for me to recite — this is no suchness apart from wisdom; apart from the Buddha that is recited, there is no mind that can recite the Buddha — this is no wisdom apart from suchness. Being neither suchness nor wisdom, there is only the one mind. Second, quiescence and illumination are hard to conceive: if one says it exists, then the very substance of the mind that can recite is itself empty, and the Buddha that is recited cannot be grasped at all; if one says it does not exist, then the mind that can recite is bright and unclouded, and the Buddha that is recited is distinctly clear; if one says it both exists and does not exist, then both the thought and the absence of thought vanish together; if one says it neither exists nor does not exist, then both the thought and the absence of thought abide together. Being not existent, it is ever quiescent; being not non-existent, it is ever illuminating; being neither both nor neither, it is neither quiescent nor illuminating, yet illuminating and quiescent. The road of words and thought is cut off, and there is nothing by which to name it; therefore there is only the one mind. At this point the feelings of subject and object dissolve and the views of existence and non-existence are exhausted; what dharma could still disturb the pure, originally-so substance? Because one has seen the truth, this is called the one-pointed mind in principle. It is indeed because practice arises from principle and principle is manifested through practice, each aiding the other, that neither may be set aside. Yet if one attends to practice and one's recitation can continue without break, the merit of entering a grade is not in vain; if one clings to principle while the mind is in fact not yet clear, one instead suffers the calamity of falling into emptiness.
” (The Yunqi Collection.)

[Investigate (ju)] Read as “ju,” meaning to inquire to the utmost. [Suchness and wisdom] “Suchness” is the dharmakāya Buddha that is recited (the Amitabha of one's own nature); “wisdom” is the mind that can recite. [Aid each other] To depend on and manifest each other. [See the truth] To see the truth. In the Śrāvaka vehicle, only one at the stage of a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna) or above can see the truth; among bodhisattvas, only one at the first ground or above can see the truth.
Concerning holding in principle, Master Lianchi cautioned: “
If one clings to principle while the mind is in fact not yet clear, one instead suffers the calamity of falling into emptiness.

” Therefore the safe and sure path is this: first achieve undisturbed one-pointed mind through holding in practice, so that rebirth is assured, and then, on that foundation, practice holding in principle so as to illumine the mind and see one's nature. In this way, not only will one avoid “the calamity of falling into emptiness,” but having first attained the one-pointed mind in practice and then turning to holding in principle, one's principle will be clear and one's work will gain strength.

Concerning the one-pointed mind in practice and the one-pointed mind in principle, Master Xingce (the tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school), in his “Admonitions on the Pure Land: Address to the Assembly on Beginning a Seven-Day Retreat of Diligence,” taught:

In seven days of reciting the name, what matters is an undisturbed one-pointed mind, without interruption and without admixture; it is not that fast reciting or much reciting is the better. Simply, neither slackly nor urgently, recite the name densely and continuously, so that the Buddha's name within the mind is distinctly clear. In putting on clothes, in eating, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, the single great name is continuous and unbroken, like the breath itself, neither scattering nor sinking. Reciting in this way, one may be said to be able to advance with one-pointed diligence in practice. But if one is a true follower of the Way
(a follower of the Way, one of those who study the Way)
, one can directly investigate and realize that all dharmas are “such”
(“such,” along with “dharma-nature” and “the ultimate,” are all different names for the true appearance of all dharmas)
, without any second appearance. That is, living beings
(sentient beings)
and Buddhas are non-dual, self and other are non-dual, the proper and the dependent retributions are non-dual, purity and impurity are non-dual, suffering and bliss are non-dual, delight
(same as “joy”)

and loathing are non-dual, grasping and rejecting are non-dual, bodhi and affliction are non-dual, and birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual. All these pairs of dharmas share one and the same appearance, one path of purity, requiring no forced arrangement
(arrangement)
, but only investigate truly as things are
(that is, simply investigate as they truly are: all dharmas are “such,” without any second appearance)

. When this investigation reaches its limit, it suddenly accords with one's own original mind. Only then does one know that putting on clothes and eating are all samādhi; that laughter, anger, and scolding are nothing but Buddha-work; and that “one-pointed mind” and “scattered mind” both become idle talk. Through the twelve periods of the day, not even a hair's breadth of difference can be found; even though one recites with utmost sincerity
(same as “recite”)

, it is the same as cursing at random; even though one practices with diligence, it is still asceticism in a dream. Only with such thorough understanding is one a true student of the Way, reciting the name with one-pointed diligence.

[The proper and the dependent retributions] The dependent retribution and the proper retribution. The lands, houses, and implements of the world, which the body depends upon, are called the “dependent retribution”; the body of the five aggregates, provisionally combined, which sentient beings receive as the result of the karma they created in the past, is called the “proper retribution.”
The former one-pointed mind
(the undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice)
seems difficult but is easy; the latter one-pointed mind
(the undisturbed one-pointed mind in principle)

seems easy but is difficult. If one can achieve only the former, rebirth is assured; if one can also achieve the latter, one may ascend to the highest grade. Yet these two kinds of one-pointed mind are both matters for ordinary beings of the vast earth
(both are things that ordinary beings are capable of)
; anyone with a mind can cultivate them. You monks and laypeople
(monastics and laity)

gathered in this hall, do not push these states up to the sages and gladly settle for what is low and inferior. Each of you must diligently urge on body and mind: in the near term, within these seven days; in the long term, within this whole life — always hold such faith and always practice such conduct. Even if you do not attain it
(even if you cannot attain the state of according with your own original mind)
, the cause you plant is still strong, and the grade in which you are born from the lotus palace
(the grade of transformation-birth within the lotus bud)
will surely not be among the middling or lower. But if, after these seven days, you ignore it as though you had never heard, and the familiar places
(that is, emotional attachments)
never fade while the unfamiliar places
(that is, reciting the Buddha's name)

still remain hard to make familiar, and the habits of ignorance and karma drag you into entanglement, then to seek merit from merely these seven days, when these seven days never reached the ground of undisturbed one-pointed mind, is exactly what is meant by being short of good roots, blessings, and conditions — how can one hope for rebirth in that land? To cause the truthful words from the Buddha's golden mouth to be doubted as deceiving falsehood — whose fault is that? You pure assembly of this seven-day retreat, I hope each of you will examine yourself and take warning and encouragement.

[Matters for ordinary beings of the vast earth] Matters belonging to ordinary beings of the vast earth. “Ordinary beings of the vast earth” are also called “ordinary beings of the pressed earth,” referring to the stage of ordinary beings. [Pressed earth (bo di)] “Pressed” (bo) means pressed upon. The “pressed earth” is the state pressed upon by the many sufferings, referring to the realm of ordinary beings. The Contemplations for Purifying the Mind says: “The ordinary being of the pressed earth has a stinking body, base and mean, with a lowly and inferior retribution.”
Question: How can one achieve the undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice?
Answer: The greatest obstacle to achieving the undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice is deluded thoughts. In the practical-study textbook of the Online Buddhist Academy of Practice as Taught,
Aware Buddha-recitation

, the causes of deluded thoughts and how to overcome them effectively are analyzed in detail, and the concrete steps and methods for achieving the undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice are explained at length. As long as one has genuine faith and earnest vows, works hard, advances step by step, and perseveres, one is certain to achieve the undisturbed one-pointed mind in practice. For details, see
The Undisturbed One-pointed Mind
The Undisturbed One-pointed Mind: Answers to a Guest's Questions
and
How to Achieve the Undisturbed One-pointed Mind
